title: The styles of recitation
hookLine: several authentic readings, passed down in chains of reciters

cards: In the Prophet's lifetime, Umar ibn al-Khattab heard a man named Hisham reciting Surah al-Furqan in the prayer, and some of the words came out differently from the way Umar had learned them from the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ himself.
Umar was so upset he could barely wait for the prayer to end. When it did, he took Hisham by his cloak and marched him straight to the Prophet.

teach.b: The Prophet asked Hisham to recite, and said: this is how it was revealed.

teach.h: THIS IS HOW IT WAS REVEALED
teach.b: He asked Umar to recite, and said again: this is how it was revealed. Then he explained that the Qur'an was revealed in seven ahruf, seven modes, so recite whichever is easy for you. The story is in Bukhari.
Scholars have discussed for centuries exactly what the seven ahruf were, and there's no single agreed answer. But within those permitted ways stand what are called the qira'at, the readings.
Each is a way of reciting the same Qur'an, traced from teacher to student in a chain back to the Prophet. The differences are small: a vowel, a letter, how long a sound is held.
In al-Fatiha, for instance, some readers recite maliki yawm al-din, King of the Day, and others maaliki, Owner of the Day. Both are accepted, and the tradition hears both as true of God.
In the tenth century, a scholar in Baghdad, Ibn Mujahid, set out seven well-known readers; later scholars recognized ten. Each has two main transmitters, whose names identify the reading.
Many printed copies today follow the reading of Hafs from Asim; in parts of North and West Africa, copies and reciters follow Warsh from Nafi'. In the tradition these aren't rival versions.
They're held to be the Qur'an itself, recited in the ways the Prophet taught.
That closes a week: Abu Bakr's collection gathered it, Uthman's copies spread it, dots and vowels helped new readers; then Arabic and translation, Pickthall and the 1934 translation, and tafsir.
And now the readings: the living voice under the page.

how: Many printed copies follow the reading of Hafs from Asim, copies in parts of North and West Africa follow Warsh from Nafi', and specialist reciters learn several readings from teachers with a chain of transmission back to the Prophet.

games.q: you're Umar. you've marched a man to the Prophet for reciting a surah differently from you. what does the Prophet say?
o: both of you recited it as it was revealed.
games.why: 'this is how it was revealed', to both. the Qur'an came in seven modes: recite whichever is easy for you.

practice: If you've heard someone recite, in a mosque, a video, a relative's kitchen, hear that voice in your mind; if you haven't, remember any voice you love hearing read aloud.
Then bring to mind another voice, somewhere else in the world, reciting the same surah at this same moment.

wordCard.voice: Qira'at. The readings: accepted ways of reciting the same Qur'an, each passed down in a chain of teachers back to the Prophet. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: many voices, one text. Maliki and maaliki, both accepted. And that's another week.
